The root-mean-square fluctuation correlation and dynamic cross-correlation matrix reconstruction confirm that contrastive learning incorporates dynamics information into the sequence embedding. We applied DPLM as a protein representation backbone for predicting diverse dynamics-related downstream tasks, including liquid-liquid phase separation, cryptic-site detection, and mutation effect on protein thermal stability. DPLM shows strong performance, especially where the evolutionary or structural signal is weak. These results show that learning the geometry of molecular motion yields transferable dynamic information that complements the evolutionary and structural features of existing PLMs.

papers.title: CucurbitAgent: An AI agent for exploring cucurbit multi-omics resources
papers.abstract: Functional genomics in crops increasingly depends on integrating information from an extensive literature and heterogeneous multi-omics datasets. Large language models (LLMs) offer a powerful approach to synthesizing these resources and revealing hidden connections across datasets; however, they frequently hallucinate, producing plausible but unsupported claims, when responding to gene-specific queries. Here, we present CucurbitAgent, an AI research agent for functional genomics in the Cucurbitaceae, a major family of horticultural crops. CucurbitAgent integrates multi-omics resources from nine cultivated cucurbit species and more than 18,000 publications, encompassing approximately 256,000 genes, tissue-resolved expression profiles, over 16 million natural genetic variants, and roughly 242,000 predicted protein structures with more than 14 million predicted binding-site residue annotations. Responses link retrieved evidence to source records, including gene entries, expression measurements, structural predictions, and literature passages. On a curated benchmark of 50 tasks assessed by domain experts under blinded conditions, CucurbitAgent achieved an overall pairwise win rate of 96.0% against nine general-purpose LLMs, based on weighted scores for factual accuracy, completeness, relevance, and traceability. The platform is freely available at https://cucurbitagent.com and supports queries in 37 languages collectively spoken by an estimated 70% or more of the world's population. CucurbitAgent not only unifies evidence retrieval and interpretation but also reveals latent associations across datasets, helping researchers formulate testable hypotheses and substantially accelerating candidate-gene research. Its framework is readily transferable to other crops and, more broadly, provides a blueprint for building specialized agents in any domain.

papers.title: ProteinBERT: a universal deep-learning model of protein sequence and function
papers.abstract: SUMMARY: Self-supervised deep language modeling has shown unprecedented success across natural language tasks, and has recently been repurposed to biological sequences. However, existing models and pretraining methods are designed and optimized for text analysis. We introduce ProteinBERT, a deep language model specifically designed for proteins. Our pretraining scheme combines language modeling with a novel task of Gene Ontology (GO) annotation prediction. We introduce novel architectural elements that make the model highly efficient and flexible to long sequences. The architecture of ProteinBERT consists of both local and global representations, allowing end-to-end processing of these types of inputs and outputs. ProteinBERT obtains near state-of-the-art performance, and sometimes exceeds it, on multiple benchmarks covering diverse protein properties (including protein structure, post-translational modifications and biophysical attributes), despite using a far smaller and faster model than competing deep-learning methods. Overall, ProteinBERT provides an efficient framework for rapidly training protein predictors, even with limited labeled data. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/nadavbra/protein_bert. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness
papers.abstract: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.

papers.title: Single-Nucleus Profiling Reveals Neuronal Metabolic Collapse During the Transition to Alzheimer's Disease Dementia
papers.abstract: Current Alzheimer's disease (AD) neuropathological metrics, including Thal phasing, and Braak staging, often do not accurately predict cognitive status: many cognitively resilient individuals have substantial pathological burdens, whereas some patients with dementia show minimal classical AD pathology. Here, we addressed this discrepancy by investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying AD dementia using single-nucleus RNA-sequencing and single-nucleus multiome datasets. To eliminate cross-modality scaling artifacts and compositional biases inherent in neurodegenerative tissues, we normalized the datasets using our novel framework, bypassing scaling issues of conventional methods that may obscure critical biological signals of interest. We identified neuron-specific suppression of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes and their upstream mitochondrial biogenesis signaling (MBS) as primary drivers of clinical dementia. By integrating multi-omic quantitative trait loci, genome-wide association studies, and epigenomic profiles, we delineated genetic and epigenetic changes underlying MBS suppression. This study provides a systematic genomic framework for understanding the mechanisms of cognitive resilience.

papers.title: Characterisation of cis-regulatory elements and genome wide enhancer prediction in Heliconiini butterflies
papers.abstract: The large-scale annotation and spatiotemporal characterisation of cis-regulatory promoters and enhancers remain limited in many non-model organisms, largely due to fragmented availability of multiomic datasets across species and developmental conditions. Heliconius butterflies, which have been used to investigate wing development and patterning, have provided key insights into the genetic architecture underlying morphological diversification and adaptive pigmentation. Despite this, we are limited in what we understand of how cis-regulatory dynamics drive phenotypic wing patterning variation. Here, by re-analysing and re-evaluating available data, we present a comprehensive new description of a cis-regulatory atlas for Heliconius wing development by integrating chromatin accessibility dynamics (ATAC-seq) with histone modification profiling (H3K27ac, H3K4me3). High-confidence peak sets enabled robust annotation of promoters and enhancers, revealing regulatory distributions consistent with canonical regulatory organisation. Promoters displayed comparatively higher conservation of transcription factor motifs, whilst enhancers exhibited greater sequence diversity, broader genomic distributions and more variable motif repertoires. Comparative analysis revealed cis-regulatory divergence to be primarily temporal, with substantial chromatin remodelling and differential histone enrichment across development, while regulatory dynamics were highly conserved between forewing and hindwing tissues. Extending these experimentally characterised regulatory landscapes, a convolutional neural network was trained for sequence-based enhancer prediction, achieving test AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.909 and 0.913, respectively. Predictions across 34 Heliconiini assemblies displayed significant enrichment within independently characterised accessible chromatin and conserved non-exonic elements (CNEEs), supporting their putative regulatory function. Overall, this study provides a large-scale characterisation of cis-regulatory dynamics and extends enhancer annotation across Heliconiini, providing a foundation for comparative investigations of regulatory conservation and diversification.

papers.title: Crowdsourcing functional cell therapy binders from generative artificial intelligence.
papers.abstract: Over thirty years ago, structural biologists established the Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction (CASP) to rigorously assess methods for predicting protein structures from amino acid sequences. Participants submitted predictions before the corresponding experimental structures became publicly available (Moult et al, 1995). This framework established a common standard against which methodological advances could be measured. Its value became particularly evident at CASP14 in 2020, when AlphaFold2 produced predictions approaching experimental accuracy for many targets (Jumper et al, ; Pereira et al, 2021). CASP’s independent, prospective assessment enabled the community to recognize the scale of this advance by providing rapid, independent validation. The next generation of CASP-like open competitions is similarly poised to help discern the impact of emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods across several domains of biology, from genomics to protein design to therapeutic discovery. The implementation and results of one such effort, the Bits to Binders competition, are described in this issue of Molecular Systems Biology, where Kosonocky, Abel and colleagues evaluated 12,000 designed proteins as recognition domains for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells (Kosonocky et al, 2026). Generative AI is advancing protein binder design. Kosonocky, Abel and colleagues report on the Bits to Binders competition, which tested 12,000 designs in engineered T cells and identified promising candidates for future cell therapies. [Figure: see text]

papers.title: SPaRTA: Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis
papers.abstract: Spatial-omics technologies provide clinicians, pathologists, and biomedical researchers with high-resolution maps of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic activity within tissues. However, querying these complex datasets often requires specialized computational expertise, limiting their accessibility to domain experts without programming experience. In the current manuscript, we develop SPaRTA (Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis), a natural-language interface that translates free-text questions into executable spatial SQL queries over such data. We release SPaRTA-Bench, comprising dataset-specific database schemas, explicit query conventions, and 7,500 question-SQL pairs validated through LLM-assisted verification and targeted human review, spanning breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, and melanoma tissue sections, and identify 15 failure modes in which a query runs but returns a wrong answer. Open-weight large language models (LLMs) of the Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and Phi families reach 10-40% execution accuracy zero-shot, and at most 61% with reasoning and execution feedback. Fine-tuning raises them to 63-77%, and they lose at most 6 percentage points on a tissue unseen in training. Execution feedback repairs queries that fail to run, but rarely queries that run and return a wrong answer.

papers.title: Digital profiling of gene expression from histology images with linearized attention
papers.abstract: Abstract Cancer is a heterogeneous disease that demands precise molecular profiling for better understanding and management. Recently, deep learning has demonstrated potentials for cost-efficient prediction of molecular alterations from histology images. While transformer-based deep learning architectures have enabled significant progress in non-medical domains, their application to histology images remains limited due to small dataset sizes coupled with the explosion of trainable parameters. Here, we develop SEQUOIA , a transformer model to predict cancer transcriptomes from whole-slide histology images. To enable the full potential of transformers, we first pre-train the model using data from 1,802 normal tissues. Then, we fine-tune and evaluate the model in 4,331 tumor samples across nine cancer types. The prediction performance is assessed at individual gene levels and pathway levels through Pearson correlation analysis and root mean square error. The generalization capacity is validated across two independent cohorts comprising 1,305 tumors. In predicting the expression levels of 25,749 genes, the highest performance is observed in cancers from breast, kidney and lung, where SEQUOIA accurately predicts the expression of 11,069, 10,086 and 8,759 genes, respectively. The accurately predicted genes are associated with the regulation of inflammatory response, cell cycles and metabolisms. While the model is trained at the tissue level, we showcase its potential in predicting spatial gene expression patterns using spatial transcriptomics datasets. Leveraging the prediction performance, we develop a digital gene expression signature that predicts the risk of recurrence in breast cancer. SEQUOIA deciphers clinically relevant gene expression patterns from histology images, opening avenues for improved cancer management and personalized therapies.

papers.title: Integrative Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Explainable AI for Disease Mechanism and Biomarker Discovery in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Invasion is an early step in the metastatic spread of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet cells within a single tumour or cell line differ in their capacity to invade, and it is unclear which transcriptional features distinguish cells that invade from those that do not. We re-analysed the public single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset GSE329526, in which ClonMapper-barcoded MDA-MB-231 cells were separated in a transwell assay into invasive (five samples, 6,289 cells) and non-invasive (five samples, 5,983 cells) fractions and compared with the parental population (one sample, 3,022 cells). An initial cell-level analysis combined Wilcoxon differential expression, an XGBoost classifier with a random cell split, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Enrichr over-representation analysis. Because cells from the same sample are not independent, we then repeated the analysis at the sample level, using differential expression on sample means (five versus five), XGBoost with cross-validation that held out whole samples, a quality-control-metric baseline model, SHAP on held-out samples and rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA). At the sample level, 6,651 of 11,727 tested genes differed between invasive and non-invasive samples (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05), including the ten top-ranked cell-level genes such as PHLDA2, ANTXR2, VIM and HMGA1 (FDR 0.0007 to 0.0022) and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) regulators TGFBR2, JAG1, SDCBP and WWTR1. With whole samples held out, XGBoost distinguished invasive from non-invasive cells with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.92 (range across folds 0.89 to 0.95); removing ribosomal and mitochondrial genes did not change performance (AUC 0.92), whereas a model using only four quality-control metrics reached 0.63, and every held-out invasive sample received a higher mean predicted probability of invasion (0.74 to 0.79) than every non-invasive sample (0.20 to 0.28). On held-out samples, SHAP ranked inflammatory and stress-response genes highest (CCL2, LGALS12, DUSP1, CXCL3, KYNU, CXCL2), and GSEA showed higher KRAS signalling (normalised enrichment score [NES] 2.30, FDR 0.001) and E2F targets (NES 1.62, FDR 0.038) and lower interferon-alpha and interferon-gamma responses (NES -1.97 and -1.65; FDR 0.001 and 0.019) in invasive samples. The ribosomal genes that dominated the original SHAP ranking were absent from the held-out ranking. Invasive MDA-MB-231 cells therefore carry a transcriptional state that is reproducible across independent transwell samples and involves EMT-related, inflammatory and proliferative programmes. Limitations include a single cell line, sequencing of the invasive and non-invasive populations in separate libraries and the absence of external validation; the candidate genes reported here are hypotheses that require confirmation in independent experiments and patient material.

papers.title: Building virtual cell dynamics that evolve with biological measurements
papers.abstract: Virtual cell models built from single-cell measurements need to predict how cells change over time, but new biological measurements often reveal dynamical relationships that existing models cannot express. Translating such measurements into dynamics therefore requires deciding what biological relation should be modeled, where it should enter the formulation and how its recovery should be validated. Here we present CellCompass, an agentic AI system that couples a scientific agent with an extensible dynamical engine for modeling state transitions and population change, along with fate and molecular readout. CellCompass reuses existing formulations when sufficient and designs, implements and refines new ones when experimental measurements introduce additional constraints. To assess this capability, we developed DynBench100, a benchmark of 100 simulated single-cell time-course scenarios with hidden dynamical ground truth. CellCompass achieved the highest aggregate performance among the tested general-purpose and biomedical agents across six dynamical tasks. Across four real single-cell studies, it retained an existing velocity-growth model to reconstruct context-dependent epithelial-mesenchymal transition and developed three new dynamical formulations for distinct experimental measurements. In drug-response data, incorporating metabolic RNA labeling reduced pulse-control identifiability error by 31.1%, revealing staged response programs and generating testable predictions for perturbing a candidate adaptive program. In hematopoietic lineage tracing, incorporating clonal barcodes improved clone-fate agreement by 54% over the strongest dynamical baseline, identifying early lineage priming among transcriptionally similar progenitors. Finally, in time-resolved CITE-seq data, CellCompass reduced future surface-protein distribution error by 13.2% for RNA-initialized trajectories, uncovering lineage-specific temporal offsets between transcriptional and protein programs. Together, CellCompass provides a framework in which virtual-cell dynamics can expand with the biological measurements used to constrain them.

papers.title: HierDTA: Hierarchical Structure-Aware Representation Learning for Drug--Target Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Drug--target affinity (DTA) prediction plays an important role in computer-aided drug discovery, where reliable computational models can help prioritize compound--protein pairs before experimental validation. A key challenge in DTA prediction is to effectively mine multi-level molecular information from drug structures while accurately modeling the binding-site environment of target proteins. To address these issues, we introduce HierDTA, a hierarchical structure-aware framework for DTA prediction. \textcolor{black}{HierDTA represents each drug as an atom--motif heterogeneous graph and introduces an augmentation module that propagates functional-motif semantics to the corresponding atoms. For proteins, kinase-domain structures are converted into residue interaction graphs. The resulting atom and residue representations are integrated using cross-attention to capture pair-specific relationships, while molecule fingerprints and pretrained ESM-2 embeddings provide complementary global information. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, HierDTA achieves superior performance on the Davis dataset across all metrics and attains the highest \(r_m^2\) of 0.791 on KIBA. It also exhibits strong generalization under cold-start settings, particularly on KIBA, where MSE is reduced by 21.7\% in the unseen-protein scenario. Ablation study and interpretability analysis supported the contributions of the hierarchical augmentation and interaction components.} Case studies further showed that HierDTA provided early enrichment of candidate bioactive compounds. These results indicate that HierDTA is an effective framework for affinity prediction and target-specific virtual screening.

papers.title: scRM: A single-cell foundation model trained on scRNA-seq reads
papers.abstract: To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at https://github.com/altos-labs/scRM.

papers.title: CMVAE: Contrastive Supervision Improves Single-Omic Latent Manifold for Breast Cancer Survival Prognosis
papers.abstract: High-dimensional omics data are vital for fore- casting patient prognosis in oncology. While deep multi-omics learning methods are increasingly popular, they suffer from data missingness and low patient overlap across modalities. Consequently, advancing single-omic representation learning re- mains a critical yet challenging research problem. Standard generative dimensionality reduction methods rely on recon- struction objectives that optimize the global manifold topology; however, overlook downstream clinical outcomes. To address these limitations, we introduce a Contrastive Masked Denois- ing Variational Autoencoder (CMVAE), a self-supervised dual- optimization framework designed to map single-omic information into a clinical outcome-aware latent space. A stochastic feature masking strategy corrupts the input omic profiles, and CMVAE is optimized to simultaneously infer missing molecular data and contrastive alignment of patient survival trajectories. We evaluate CMVAE using leak-proof five-fold stratified cross-validation on the TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma (BRCA) cohort. The method outperforms traditional unsupervised methods, achieving an AUROC of 0.7397 {+/-} 0.0239 on patient prognosis. Further analysis demonstrates a highly significant (p < 0.0001) risk stratification among low vs. high risk groups. Beyond comparing within single-omic methods, CMVAE outperforms six state-of- the-art multi-omics survival baselines by a minimum of 3%. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/CMVAE. Note: Accepted at the IEEE BIBM 2026 workshop RLPD-Bio (Representation Learning and Pattern Discovery for Bioinformatics and Biomedicine).

papers.title: A compact motif vocabulary is differentially interpreted across human cell types
papers.abstract: How a common genome generates diverse human cell types may depend less on distinct cis-regulatory vocabularies than on context-dependent use of a shared one. We have developed CNN-CR, an interpretable neural network that learns regulatory motifs while predicting gene expression across 116 human biosamples. Promoter regulation proves highly compressible: dozens of recurrent motif families retain most of the predictive information of much larger cell-type-specific vocabularies and generalize to cellular contexts excluded from their discovery. These motifs are conserved at their binding sites and enriched at fine-mapped regulatory variants. Cellular context acts at two levels: chromatin state gates which motif instances are available for regulatory use, whereas reader identity determines how accessible motifs are interpreted. ChIP-seq data reveal frequent shifts in reader occupancy across cell types, and genome-scale perturbations support corresponding context-dependent reader functions. Thus, regulatory diversity can emerge through differential access to and interpretation of a compact shared DNA vocabulary.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Dual-Target Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery Under Strict Homology Constraints
papers.abstract: The worldwide escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe challenge to modern public health, necessitating novel classes of therapeutic agents. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent highly promising alternatives to small-molecule antibiotics due to their co-evolutionary resilience and rapid membrane disruption dynamics. However, translating computational AMP leads into clinical drug candidates remains bottlenecked by off-target cytotoxicity, predominantly hemolytic activity against mammalian erythrocytes. Although pretrained foundational protein language models (PLMs) have rapidly advanced molecular property prediction, current architectures frequently isolate antibacterial potency and cytotoxicity into disconnected single-task pipelines or succumb to catastrophic performance drops under strict homology-controlled evaluations. Recently, the Quantitative Mapping of Antimicrobial Peptides (QMAP) benchmark proposed that frozen PLM embeddings show weak linearly accessible features for hemolytic activity (HC50) resulting in poor rank correlation ({rho} < 0.25) on out-of-distribution sequence splits. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end multi-task parameter-efficient transfer learning framework designed to simultaneously optimize antibacterial potency and minimize mammalian cytotoxicity without sequence leakage. Built upon ESM-2 (150M), our architecture incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into self-attention projections, fine-tuning approx 0.70% of model weights. To restore gradient interference originating from disparate membrane lysis mechanisms, we implement an adaptive multi-task loss guided by Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. Evaluated across predefined QMAP benchmark splits enforcing a 60% maximal sequence identity threshold, our joint architecture remarkably outperforms conventional linear probes, tree-based regressors, and frozen foundational models. The framework achieves an E. coli potency rank correlation of {rho} = 0.6132 (r = 0.6816) and successfully elevates hemolytic toxicity correlation to {rho} = 0.5374 (r = 0.5541). To establish real world utility, we deploy the optimized joint network to screen a curated in silico library of 749 de-novo designed peptides, successfully isolating selective cationic-amphipathic candidates possessing Therapeutic Indices (TI = HC50/MIC) up to 144.03 while effectively deprioritizing broadly lytic motifs (TI < 2.0). These findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient adaptation unlocks fine-grained bioactive structural semantics in foundational PLMs, providing an accurate, scalable framework for therapeutic peptide engineering.

papers.title: LabWeaver: reliable agentic data analysis grounded in laboratory knowled
papers.abstract: Agentic systems powered by large language models are rapidly automating biological data analysis. However, their reliability remains questionable because they often overlook experimental context, such as disease domain and experimental protocol. Existing agentic systems organize context around individual users and projects, whereas research is organized around laboratories whose projects share experimental context. As a result, experimental context learned in one project remains unavailable to related projects. We introduce LabWeaver, an agentic data analysis framework with a laboratory-organized architecture of three tiers: laboratory, user and project. Further, LabWeaver distills experimental context into laboratory memory and skills, which are shared across users and projects after human-gated review. To isolate the contribution of experimental context, we analyzed a synovial sarcoma single-cell RNA-seq dataset in two sessions that differed only in whether laboratory memory and skills were available. The context-free session lost the fusion reporter at read alignment and misannotated the tumor cells. In contrast, the context-enabled session recovered reporter expression and resolved five fusion-anchored tumor cell states.

papers.title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
papers.abstract: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

papers.title: IsoAlign: Isoform-Aware DNA-Protein Alignment via Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning DNA sequence representations, yet existing self-supervised pretraining strategies overlook alternative splicing and underperform compared to specialized models. To address this gap, we introduce IsoAlign, a multimodal framework that grounds genomic pretraining in isoform-aware DNA-protein alignment to learn biologically meaningful representations. IsoAlign aligns transcripts to their corresponding protein isoforms, capturing both coding sequences and broader regulatory contexts, using two Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA): DNA-Protein JEPA (DP-JEPA), which predicts protein representations from DNA using contrastive alignment, and Isoform-Masked JEPA (IM-JEPA), which models relationships among alternative isoforms of the same gene through masked protein prediction. We evaluate the learned DNA representations of these architectures across a multi-metric evaluation suite spanning tasks, including the prediction of pathogenicity, fitness, gene expression, and TF binding. Our results demonstrate that isoform-aware cross-modal alignment using JEPA significantly improves functional representations and downstream performance, establishing a promising direction for GFM pretraining.

papers.title: Longitudinal AI Models Predict Cancer Adverse Events
papers.abstract: Clinical interventions for cancer treatment toxicities can reduce morbidity, mortality, and healthcare cost, if high risk patients can be identified. We developed SPARC, a transformer-based foundation model, using real-world, longitudinal, routinely collected health measurements, to predict adverse event risk. Pre-training and fine-tuning SPARC on 101,920,379 measurements from 224,047 patients with cancer led to state-of-the-art performance at predicting cancer-related adverse events on (i) held-out data from the development cohort, (ii) a prospective validation cohort from the same center (Npatients=23,126), (iii) multiple publicly available external datasets (Npatients=26,012), and (iv) external, multi-hospital cohorts (Npatients=562,620, 206,840). SPARC generalized to multiple external centers and identified patients most likely to benefit from an intervention (G-CSF). Pooled multi-institution, more than single-institution, fine-tuning improved generalizability. We release SPARC as a community resource. Our results highlight the utility of AI time series models in oncologic management.

papers.title: Interactome-based deep learning and path-level decomposition reveal TGFβ-IFNα competition in MASH
papers.abstract: Dysregulated signaling drives Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis (MASH) through a complex crosstalk between pro- and anti-fibrotic cues. We previously observed potential competition between IFN-mediated JAK-STAT signaling and TGF{beta} in modulating MASH fibrosis, but the precise mechanism of that competition, and whether it can act directly on hepatocytes, is yet unknown. We used DT-LEMBAS, an interactome-based deep learning framework, training an ensemble of 50 models on drug-induced transcriptomics from primary human hepatocytes. The ensemble captured transcriptional changes induced by simulated receptor knockouts and aligned predicted profiles with known TGF{beta}- and IFN-induced phenotypes. Systematic simulations demonstrate their competitive modulation of MASH phenotype scores benchmarked against human cohorts. To extract mechanistic insights, we developed a gradient-based approach, where we computed the Jacobian of the used recurrent signaling network and applied chain rule decomposition to identify a four-node module of SMAD3, TP63, STAT2, and STAT3. Mechanistic hypotheses involving these canonical and non-canonical TF mediators were experimentally validated in primary hepatocyte spheroids. This work establishes a generalizable and scalable approach to decode large signaling neural networks into interpretable biological subnetworks.

papers.title: An agent-built, verified atlas of public spatial transcriptomics shows that breadth across studies drives transfer and reproducibility
papers.abstract: Public spatial transcriptomics data are deposited study by study, in formats that differ from one laboratory to the next, and no resource has yet indexed or verified them as a whole. Here we present SpatialDataAgent-DB, an atlas built from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) by SpatialDataAgent, a workflow in which language-model agents do the work and every output is checked rather than trusted. An assay index covering all 298,179 GEO series identifies 2,411 spatial series, which gives public spatial data an explicit denominator. For each series, an agent writes conversion code instead of editing the data directly, and a frozen, rule-based scorer recomputes every released value from the source files. In a held-out test, the scorer rejected all 1,231 corrupted copies. We also visually reviewed every released sample, including the 4,386 H&E-registered Visium samples of our earlier HESRT release. SpatialDataAgent-DB contains 12,163 samples from 12 platforms and 42 species in a single format, each with its provenance and defect flags. Its 8,211 image-paired samples are 5.9 times as many as in the next image-paired resource, and at least 71% of all samples are absent from five existing catalogues. Without batch correction, sequencing-based samples group by organ more than by platform: with platforms balanced, organ explains 32% of the variance of human pseudobulk profiles and platform 13% (mouse, 47% and 18%). We then used the atlas in two applications. Image-to-expression models trained on it transfer to unseen studies, and their accuracy rises steadily with training data and, at a fixed number of patches, with the number of training studies over the range tested (for H&E, Pearson r gains 0.0056 per doubling of training patches up to 524,288); 11 of 13 forecasts locked in advance were confirmed. Adding studies helps more than adding patches from the same studies, because each study leaves a fingerprint in its images. Intent-based search over the same index assembled 70 single-cell dementia studies, and the replication of disease signatures in held-out studies rose steadily with the number of studies (direction agreement averaged over 28 held-out studies, 63% with one study and 77% with 16). In both applications, performance kept rising with the number of independent studies, which a complete and verified atlas is built to provide.

papers.title: Generative augmentation recovers prognostic disease signatures from underpowered transcriptomic datasets
papers.abstract: Identifying reliable gene-expression signatures from small transcriptomic datasets remains challenging. We present GeneLift, a framework that augments underpowered datasets using Gaussian mixture modelling in an analytically invertible latent space, retains genes reproducibly recovered across augmentations, and dates each against the literature using EvidenceClock, a Bayesian PubMed co-occurrence score, as antecedent, subsequent or unreported. Across 52 microarray and RNA-seq datasets spanning breast cancer, ovarian cancer, diabetes, sepsis and tuberculosis, GeneLift recovered candidate genes missed by standard differential expression analysis in all five diseases, including 326 in breast cancer and 976 in ovarian cancer. These candidates carried disease-specific literature support, including genes reported up to 18 years later such as the survival-associated ARL4D, and stratified overall survival in independent cohorts: TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC (log-rank P=6e-21 and 1e-42) and TCGA high-grade serous ovarian cancer (P=1e-37). In benchmarking, Gaussian mixture modelling outperformed more computationally intensive transformer-based generative adversarial networks. Together, GeneLift and EvidenceClock provide an efficient, reproducible framework for recovering prognostically informative signatures from underpowered transcriptomic studies.

papers.title: Small molecule structure elucidation from NMR spectra with generative and reasoning models
papers.abstract: Elucidating the structures of unknown small molecules remains a major challenge in chemistry, pharmacology, and drug discovery. While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the gold standard for structure elucidation, interpreting spectra remains labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge to navigate the vast space of possible structures. Here, we present an AI system for rapid, automated de novo structure elucidation that combines a molecular generative model with a scientific reasoning agent. Its generative component, ChefNMR2, is an atomic flow-matching model that predicts small-molecule structures from molecular formulae and one-dimensional 1H and 13C NMR spectra. ChefNMR2-Agent augments our generative model with large language models (LLMs) to reason over and refine candidate structures. Across diverse benchmarks, ChefNMR2 substantially outperforms existing tools, offering calibrated confidence estimates and two to three orders of magnitude faster inference than frontier LLMs. We use ChefNMR2-Agent to elucidate the structures of four novel natural products, matching human-chemist accuracy in a fraction of the time. Our work demonstrates how specialized generative models and general-purpose reasoning agents can unite to solve challenging scientific inverse problems and accelerate NMR structure elucidation, thus opening new possibilities for AI-driven small-molecule discovery across diverse disciplines.

papers.title: GENA-LM: a family of open-source foundational DNA language models for long sequences
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in genomics, propelled by artificial intelligence, have unlocked unprecedented capabilities in interpreting genomic sequences, mitigating the need for exhaustive experimental analysis of complex, intertwined molecular processes inherent in DNA function. A significant challenge, however, resides in accurately decoding genomic sequences, which inherently involves comprehending rich contextual information dispersed across thousands of nucleotides. To address this need, we introduce GENA language model (GENA-LM), a suite of transformer-based foundational DNA language models capable of handling input lengths up to 36 000 base pairs. Notably, integrating the newly developed recurrent memory mechanism allows these models to process even larger DNA segments. We provide pre-trained versions of GENA-LM, including multispecies and taxon-specific models, demonstrating their capability for fine-tuning and addressing a spectrum of complex biological tasks with modest computational demands. While language models have already achieved significant breakthroughs in protein biology, GENA-LM showcases a similarly promising potential for reshaping the landscape of genomics and multi-omics data analysis. All models are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AIRI-Institute/GENA_LM) and on HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/AIRI-Institute). In addition, we provide a web service (https://dnalm.airi.net/) allowing user-friendly DNA annotation with GENA-LM models.

papers.title: DBAASP V4: condition-resolved bioactivity and chemical structures for data-driven peptide and peptidomimetic discovery.
papers.abstract: The current peptide renaissance-driven by metagenomic and proteomic mining, molecular de-extinction, protein language models, and generative or evolutionary design-is producing millions of candidates, but useful machine learning depends on experimentally anchored, context-rich labels. The Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP) is a manually curated resource linking peptides and peptidomimetics to quantitative antimicrobial, antibiofilm, anticancer, hemolytic, and mammalian-cell cytotoxicity measurements and their experimental conditions. DBAASP v4 contains >25 000 entries and extends the resource from a sequence-centered database to a structure-aware repository. Major additions include systematic SMILES representations, enhanced annotation of intrachain bonds and ring architectures, dedicated antibiofilm, and synergy records, PubChem links, >9200 molecular-dynamics trajectories, and new prediction services. The condition-resolved data support supervised learning, strain-, and target-specific models, model calibration, and surrogate fitness functions for genetic algorithms. SMILES representations further enable modeling of noncanonical peptides and peptidomimetics that cannot be adequately described by sequence alone. DBAASP therefore complements large peptide catalogues by providing the experimentally curated activity and structure layers, needed to convert sequence information into testable predictions, design, and optimization of biologically active compounds. DBAASP v4 is freely available at https://dbaasp.org.

papers.title: Digital twins forecast individual immune trajectories
papers.abstract: The human immune system differs markedly between individuals and changes in response to infection, vaccination and treatment. AI virtual cells are being built to simulate cellular responses to perturbation. Yet these models, like most immune-response predictors, describe each person by a single pre-challenge measurement and forecast change from patterns pooled across people. Digital twins, updated with every new observation of an individual, could forecast how that person's immune state changes. Here we present ImmuneTwins, which builds these twins from single-cell profiles by personalizing a shared virtual-cell model with each individual's observations. In two external populations, ImmuneTwins reduced immune-age error by 32% and 42% relative to the best existing method. During repeated influenza vaccination, its twins predicted the direction of immune-cell change 35% more accurately than the best published method, and their error fell by 27% as observations accumulated. The twins revealed that immune cells and plasma proteins recover about half their deviation from a persistent personal reference within 90 days, whereas response size varies between challenges. They further localized B-cell remodelling in exceptional longevity and anticipated patient-specific immune trajectories during myeloma treatment. These results establish virtual-cell digital twins for forecasting individual immune change and identifying each person's characteristic immune features.

papers.title: Predicting Pathway Dependency in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma from Hallmark Transcriptomic Features
papers.abstract: Despite frequent pathway activation, targeted molecular therapy remains limited in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), highlighting the need to distinguish activation from dependence. Dependency is functional, context-specific, and coupled; mutations or expression alone cannot establish it. No validated framework identifies tumor pathway dependencies from baseline molecular profiles. We developed a transcriptome-based framework to infer pathway dependency in HNSCC. Nine Elastic Net models used 50 MSigDB Hallmark activity profiles from 953 GDSC cell lines and drug responses pooled across compounds annotated to each pathway. Cross-validated R2 ranged from 0.17 (IGF1R) to 0.48 (P53); leave-one-pathway-out validation retained rank agreement (Spearman {rho} = 0.19-0.56) for pathways with no drug response observed during training. We validated the models using pharmacological, genomic, and proteomic data, then applied them to TCGA-HNSC (n = 565) and GSE65858 (n = 256), examining HPV status, age, stage, tobacco history, and CD8+ infiltration. Seven of nine pathways were higher in HPV+ tumors and replicated directionally in GSE65858. Among TP53-wild-type tumors, HPV remained linked to greater P53 dependency ({beta} = +0.37, q = 0.010); HPV+ tumors also had higher p53 transcriptional activity, suggesting residual p53 function despite E6 expression. The codependency signature had a dominant global axis (PC1 = 62.3% variance; Cronbach's = 0.91), replicated across cohorts (Tucker congruence = 0.996), but largely reflected CD8+ T-cell infiltration ({rho} = 0.80). The framework uses RNA-sequenced bulk tumor cohorts to assess baseline transcriptome-based dependencies and match pathway-directed agents to likely responders before treatment. It is not prognostic.

papers.title: Network-guided identification of candidate biomarkers for COPD-associated comorbidities using deep learning and real-world transcriptomic data
papers.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) frequently coexists with infections, metabolic disease, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory lung injury and lung cancer. Molecular markers derived by comparing a comorbidity with healthy controls need not identify the transition from an established COPD state to that comorbidity. We therefore developed a two-stage computational strategy that asks a narrower question: which proteins can distinguish COPD samples from samples annotated with a specific COPD-associated comorbidity? First, a Human Protein Network (HPN; 17,302 proteins and 492,195 relationships) was encoded by 20 graph-derived features. A convolutional-neural-network ensemble, termed the functional-distance model (FDM), was trained on known drug-target-indication relationships. Stored training-set predictions yielded an apparent balanced accuracy of 0.811 and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.627; these values describe resubstitution performance and are not an independent estimate of generalization. The COPD-centred network search evaluated 2,645 nearby proteins and retained 224 candidates using a COPD FDM score above 0.50. Candidate expression was then tested in independently assembled public patient-derived transcriptomic data using simple one-feature classifiers and cross-validation. The resulting exploratory panel contained GTF2I for bacterial infection, UBXN7 for type 2 diabetes, LIFR for hypertension, SRGN for lung neoplasm and FGF4 for pneumonitis. Across the saved cross-validation predictions, balanced accuracy ranged from 0.838 to 0.970 and MCC from 0.726 to 0.941. SRGN has direct experimental support in non-small-cell lung cancer, whereas the remaining candidates have varying indirect mechanistic support and should be regarded as hypotheses rather than established disease biomarkers. This work demonstrates an orthogonal discovery framework in which network-based functional prioritization and patient-derived molecular discrimination constrain one another. Its main contribution is methodological: it provides a reusable strategy for generating comorbidity-specific biomarker hypotheses from an index-disease state. Prospective longitudinal cohorts are required before claims of progression prediction or clinical utility can be made.

papers.title: DeepTTA: a transformer-based model for predicting cancer drug response
papers.abstract: Identifying new lead molecules to treat cancer requires more than a decade of dedicated effort. Before selected drug candidates are used in the clinic, their anti-cancer activity is generally validated by in vitro cellular experiments. Therefore, accurate prediction of cancer drug response is a critical and challenging task for anti-cancer drugs design and precision medicine. With the development of pharmacogenomics, the combination of efficient drug feature extraction methods and omics data has made it possible to use computational models to assist in drug response prediction. In this study, we propose DeepTTA, a novel end-to-end deep learning model that utilizes transformer for drug representation learning and a multilayer neural network for transcriptomic data prediction of the anti-cancer drug responses. Specifically, DeepTTA uses transcriptomic gene expression data and chemical substructures of drugs for drug response prediction. Compared to existing methods, DeepTTA achieved higher performance in terms of root mean square error, Pearson correlation coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient on multiple test sets. Moreover, we discovered that anti-cancer drugs bortezomib and dactinomycin provide a potential therapeutic option with multiple clinical indications. With its excellent performance, DeepTTA is expected to be an effective method in cancer drug design.

papers.title: Identification of driver genes for critical forms of COVID-19 in a deeply phenotyped young patient cohort
papers.abstract: Abstract The etiopathogenesis of severe COVID-19 remains unknown. Indeed given major confounding factors (age and co-morbidities), true drivers of this condition have remained elusive. Here, we employ an unprecedented multi-omics analysis, combined with artificial intelligence, in a young patient cohort where major co-morbidities have been excluded at the onset. Here, we established a three-tier cohort of individuals younger than 50 years without major comorbidities. These included 47 “critical” (in the ICU under mechanical ventilation) and 25 “non-critical” (in a noncritical care ward) COVID-19 patients as well as 22 healthy individuals. The analyses included whole-genome sequencing, whole-blood RNA sequencing, plasma and blood mononuclear cells proteomics, cytokine profiling and high-throughput immunophenotyping. An ensemble of machine learning, deep learning, quantum annealing and structural causal modeling led to key findings. Critical patients were characterized by exacerbated inflammation, perturbed lymphoid/myeloid compartments, coagulation and viral cell biology. Within a unique gene signature that differentiated critical from noncritical patients, several driver genes promoted severe COVID-19 among which the upregulated metalloprotease ADAM9 was key. This gene signature was replicated in an independent cohort of 81 critical and 73 recovered COVID-19 patients, as were ADAM9 transcripts, soluble form and proteolytic activity. Ex vivo ADAM9 inhibition affected SARS-CoV-2 uptake and replication in human lung epithelial cells. In conclusion, within a young, otherwise healthy, COVID-19 cohort, we provide the landscape of biological perturbations in vivo where a unique gene signature differentiated critical from non-critical patients. The key driver, ADAM9 , interfered with SARS-CoV-2 biology. A repositioning strategy for anti-ADAM9 therapeutic is feasible. One sentence summary Etiopathogenesis of severe COVID19 in a young patient population devoid of comorbidities.

papers.title: Multimodal data-driven clustering analysis of heart failure patients identifies two distinct patterns of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: Results from the PACIFIC-PRESERVED study.
papers.abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for over half of heart failure cases but remains poorly defined due to its clinical heterogeneity. In the prospective PACIFIC-Preserved cohort (NCT04189029, n = 155), we applied multimodal deep phenotyping, including high-throughput proteomics, and unsupervised machine learning to identify biologically distinct HFpEF subgroups. Multiview clustering revealed two major HFpEF phenogroups: PEF1, characterized by inflammatory signaling, TNF receptor activation, cardio-skeletal injury, and greater renal dysfunction; and PEF2, marked by endothelial stress and milder perturbations. Conventional diagnostics alone could not reliably distinguish these subgroups, but a multimodal classifier integrating clinical, imaging, and proteomic variables achieved high predictive accuracy (F1-score 0.87). External validation in the MEDIA-DHF cohort (n = 456) confirmed that PEF1 was independently associated with adverse outcomes (adjusted HR 2.27, 95% CI 1.04-4.94). These findings establish a classifier-driven, biologically informed stratification of HFpEF, providing a framework for precision medicine in heart failure.

papers.title: Protein large language model-assisted one-to-one gene homology mapping in cross-species single-cell transcriptome integration.
papers.abstract: Cross-species integration of single-cell transcriptomes requires establishing gene correspondences to enable comparative analysis of expression profiles across organisms. Current approaches predominantly rely on Ensembl homology tables; although gene-family expansion and contraction can reflect biologically meaningful evolutionary divergence, default many-to-many mappings can overweight expanded gene-family signals during integration and generate mapping-associated microclusters that lack clear cell-type identity, thereby complicating direct cell-type alignment. Although restricting mappings to a one-to-one scheme suppresses such artifacts, it reduces the number of homology gene pairs by ∼8% (about 900 pairs). To address this limitation, we develop a protein large language model (pLLM)-based gene homology mapping strategy that boosts the number of homology gene pairs. By enforcing a one-to-one mapping constraint and integrating pLLM-derived representations with sequence similarity, we construct a fused mapping approach, which achieves top performance in a comprehensive benchmark based on a curated cross-species atlas spanning nine data sets, 11 species, and more than 3.2 million cells. Our method further identifies previously unannotated cell-type marker pairs, facilitating novel cross-species marker discovery. These results establish a robust framework for gene homology mapping in cross-species transcriptome integration, improving both accuracy and biological interpretability.

papers.title: CytoVI: deep generative modeling of antibody-based single cell data.
papers.abstract: Antibody-based single-cell technologies, such as flow cytometry, mass cytometry and CITE-seq, have become widely used in clinical diagnostics and basic research; however, their analysis is complicated by technical noise, batch effects, platform differences and restricted antibody panels. Here we present CytoVI, a probabilistic generative model for statistically rigorous unified analysis of antibody-based single-cell data. CytoVI generates informative cell embeddings, imputes missing measurements, performs differential protein expression testing and automates annotation of cells in a single probabilistic model. We applied CytoVI to build an integrated B cell maturation atlas spanning 350 proteins and identified proteins associated with immunoglobulin class-switching. In a cohort of patients with B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma profiled by flow cytometry and CITE-seq, CytoVI uncovered disease-associated T cell states. CytoVI is available as open-source software at scvi-tools.org .

papers.title: Function-preserving watermarking of AI-generated proteins.
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) models are revolutionizing biology, with tools such as AlphaFold 3 and protein design models accelerating breakthroughs in protein structure prediction and the creation of new functional proteins1. Tracking and establishing the provenance of AI-generated protein sequences and structures is becoming increasingly important to tackle a range of emerging challenges, including biosecurity and concerns about information veracity2-4. Here we introduce SynthIDBio, a family of methods for watermarking protein sequences and structures to establish the provenance of those generated with AI. SynthIDBio-sequence actively embeds a watermark into protein sequences while preserving function. We demonstrate this by creating watermarked, functional designed protein binders with binding affinity comparable with non-watermarked counterparts and near-perfect watermark detection accuracy. Furthermore, SynthIDBio-structure, a fine-tuned AlphaFold3 model, embeds an imperceptible watermark into biomolecular structures. Our work is a proof-of-concept that function-preserving biological watermarking is feasible, introducing a potential tool for provenance in the rapidly expanding era of AI-driven biological engineering.

papers.title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
papers.abstract: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

papers.title: HELIOS: A spatial omics-informed multi-organ cell atlas enables AI-based tumour microenvironment profiling and biomarker discovery from routine histopathology
papers.abstract: Spatial omics defines tumour microenvironments with high biological resolution but remains difficult to scale across large clinical cohorts. We developed HELIOS (H&E Learning Informed by Omics and Spatial Profiling), which transfers spatial-omics-derived cell identities into routine haematoxylin and eosin histology for interpretable single-cell tumour microenvironment profiling. HELIOS integrates 12.9 million cells from 60 specimens across 13 tissue types and four spatial profiling platforms, spanning eight epithelial, immune, stromal, and vascular populations. The resulting multiclass detector generalised across independent histopathology benchmarks. Applied to colorectal, breast, and lung cancers, HELIOS recapitulated molecular subtype-associated microenvironment states and identified prognostic immune and stromal phenotypes. Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes were consistently associated with favourable outcomes, whereas neutrophil and fibroblast phenotypes showed cancer-specific associations. HELIOS-derived features remained prognostic after adjustment for clinicopathological and molecular variables. These findings demonstrate that spatial omics can provide scalable biological supervision for extracting clinically relevant tumour microenvironment features from routine H&E, supporting scalable risk stratification and biomarker development across clinical cohorts and retrospective pathology archives.

papers.title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
papers.abstract: A central goal of biology is to predict the dynamics of multicellular systems. Lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins, etc.) could inform these predictions, but how best to leverage it remains unclear. Here we introduce lineage inpainting, a generative modeling approach that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to model cell state dynamics across lineage trees. Applied to a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, it recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including multiple transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages are drawn to a common state. Despite being fit on unperturbed development, lineage inpainting can generate hypotheses about perturbation responses by simulating counterfactuals. These simulations agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response. Our results show that lineage information provides a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

papers.title: TACFormer: Transformer-Based Generative Model for Target-Conditioned De Novo PROTAC Design
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) represents a fundamental shift in drug discovery, moving beyond traditional target inhibition toward the event-driven removal of disease-causing proteins. A prominent strategy for TPD is the use of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), heterobifunctional molecules that selectively route a protein of interest (POI) to the ubiquitin-proteasome system for degradation. While PROTAC design still relies heavily on trial-and-error synthesis and experimental testing, deep generative models offer a promising means to explore PROTAC chemical space in silico and generate novel molecules. However, many existing generative methods formulate PROTAC design primarily as a linker-generation problem, with POI-binding (warhead) and E3-ligase-binding components fixed in advance. This restricts exploration of the full PROTAC chemical space and often leaves the POI implicit through the predefined warhead, rather than using protein-level information as an explicit conditioning signal during generation. To address these limitations, we propose TACFormer: a transformer-based generative model for target-aware de novo PROTAC design. The model conditions a GPT-style molecular decoder on pretrained ESM-2 representations of POI sequences, allowing POI-level information to steer full-molecule generation. Our results show that TACFormer generates highly novel and chemically diverse PROTACs while showing consistent POI-dependent shifts in generated chemical space. In particular, molecules generated under specific target conditions preferentially populate chemical neighborhoods associated with POIs in the held-out dataset, while extrapolating to novel chemotypes. By natively integrating biological context into the generative process, TACFormer moves PROTAC design toward a more biology-informed exploration of degrader chemical space.

papers.title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
papers.abstract: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that non-HVG handling is a central determinant of privacy: directly copying non-HVG values leads to severe leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious design choices throughout preprocessing, generation, and post-processing.

papers.title: Integrate multi-omics data with biological interaction networks using Multi-view Factorization AutoEncoder (MAE)
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Comprehensive molecular profiling of various cancers and other diseases has generated vast amounts of multi-omics data. Each type of -omics data corresponds to one feature space, such as gene expression, miRNA expression, DNA methylation, etc. Integrating multi-omics data can link different layers of molecular feature spaces and is crucial to elucidate molecular pathways underlying various diseases. Machine learning approaches to mining multi-omics data hold great promises in uncovering intricate relationships among molecular features. However, due to the "big p, small n" problem (i.e., small sample sizes with high-dimensional features), training a large-scale generalizable deep learning model with multi-omics data alone is very challenging. RESULTS: We developed a method called Multi-view Factorization AutoEncoder (MAE) with network constraints that can seamlessly integrate multi-omics data and domain knowledge such as molecular interaction networks. Our method learns feature and patient embeddings simultaneously with deep representation learning. Both feature representations and patient representations are subject to certain constraints specified as regularization terms in the training objective. By incorporating domain knowledge into the training objective, we implicitly introduced a good inductive bias into the machine learning model, which helps improve model generalizability. We performed extensive experiments on the TCGA datasets and demonstrated the power of integrating multi-omics data and biological interaction networks using our proposed method for predicting target clinical variables. CONCLUSIONS: To alleviate the overfitting problem in deep learning on multi-omics data with the "big p, small n" problem, it is helpful to incorporate biological domain knowledge into the model as inductive biases. It is very promising to design machine learning models that facilitate the seamless integration of large-scale multi-omics data and biomedical domain knowledge for uncovering intricate relationships among molecular features and clinical features.

papers.title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable SI Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generating novel AMPs with desired properties using generative SI (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable SI (XSI) methods to validate the GenSI model and derive biological insights. In this work, we fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. To advance the interpretability and reliability of the generative model, we applied Explainable SI (XSI) techniques. Specifically, we used a probing classifier and a regressor to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we validated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. Overall, these methods provide mechanistic insight into the model's decision-making process, offering a principled basis for trusting the sequences it generates rather than treating the model as a black box. Candidate sequences were filtered based on predicted Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) along with human insights into the structural activities of the AMPs in bacterial membranes, and a final set of peptides was selected for experimental testing. Biological assays for determining MIC confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, with fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements providing structural insight. With our XSI approach, we are able to reveal correlations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties of these sequences to bacterial membrane mimics, that directly correlate with biological activities in cell-based assays. This builds confidence in that the learned amino acid interdependencies as applied to AMPs carries physico-chemical meaning and is relevant for discoveries of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can serve as effective and transparent tools for rational AMP discovery.

papers.title: Physiological mapping and prediction reveal stress-responsive translation initiation landscapes
papers.abstract: Translation initiation defines the protein output of the transcriptome, but its physiological dynamics in cells and tissues remain incompletely characterized. Here we develop TISCA2, an inhibitor-free method that captures eIF5B-associated initiating ribosomes to map translation initiation sites genome-wide. By directly identifying start sites rather than inferring translation from elongating-ribosome periodicity, TISCA2 improves the detection of short and overlapping translons. Translation of a subset of TISCA2-identified translons is supported by N-terminal proteomics and HLA-I immunopeptidomics. The arsenite-induced integrated stress response broadly redistributes start-site usage, reducing upstream initiation in favor of downstream initiation. TISCA2 further reveals tissue-specific initiation landscapes in vivo, with increased detection of downstream candidate start sites in the testis. Finally, we develop IncepTIS, a sequence-based deep learning model that predicts position-resolved and condition-dependent initiation landscapes. IncepTIS-guided optimization generates de novo mRNA 5' leaders with stress-responsive initiation patterns. Together, TISCA2 and IncepTIS provide an experimental and computational framework for mapping, predicting and engineering translation initiation in mammalian cells and tissues.

papers.title: Deep Lineage: Single-cell lineage tracing and fate inference using deep learning.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing and lineage tracing techniques have provided valuable insights into the temporal changes in gene expression during development, tumor progression, and disease onset. However, there are few computational methods available to analyze this information to help understand multicellular dynamics. We introduce Deep Lineage, a deep-learning method for analyzing time-series single-cell RNA sequencing with matched lineage tracing data. Our method accurately predicts early cell fate biases and gene expression profiles at different time points within a clone, surpassing existing methods in fate prediction accuracy. We further validate our model using LineageSim, a fate-aware lineage simulator, demonstrating robustness to technical noise such as barcode dropout and clone misidentification. Additionally, we apply Deep Lineage to in silico perturbations in cellular reprogramming and hematopoiesis to identify key genes and pathways associated with cell fate determination and propose testable perturbation hypotheses for experimental follow-up.

papers.title: Generative design of functional disordered regions in a developmental transcription factor
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in protein structure design have not translated to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of how IDR sequence encodes function. Here, we use stem cell differentiation as a model to map functional sequence features in the IDR of transcription factor RUNX2. We show that RUNX2 requires its C-terminal IDR to bind chromatin and regulate gene expression during osteogenesis. Surprisingly, linear IDR sequence is dispensable, and instead features of the conformational ensemble predict function. We develop an algorithm for rational IDR design based on biophysical principles, and use it to generate functional IDRs de novo. Together, these results illustrate the central role for TF IDRs in chromatin binding and extend generative protein design beyond the folded proteome.

papers.title: Understanding Gene Expression-to-Image Learning: Spatial Structure and Information Fidelity
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables cell-level analysis of biological heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles remains challenging. Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) offers an effective learning strategy by arranging gene values on pixel grids for convolutional neural networks, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We study GE2I on full-transcriptome data while keeping the network and training procedure fixed. Our results reveal a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity. Structured mappings produce smooth, low-frequency patterns that support faster early optimization, whereas assigning multiple genes to the same pixel obscures expression differences and can reduce predictive performance. This trade-off explains why random mappings can compete with structured layouts when many genes are represented. One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across the tested visual backbones even when image smoothness decreases. We further find that the benefits of pretraining and augmentation depend on the backbone and mapping. These findings provide practical guidance for pixel allocation and the transfer of vision priors to gene expression data.

papers.title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
papers.abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

papers.title: De novo transformer modeling improves recovery of genetic cell types from sparse single-cell RNA sequencing
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) simultaneously provides gene-expression profiles and genetic variants from individual cells, creating an opportunity to relate cellular phenotypes to their somatic evolutionary histories. However, delineating genetic types (GTs) from scRNA-seq remains difficult because most bases remain undetected in each cellular genome and are accompanied by false-positive and false-negative base calls.
